title: Drone Strikes Surge in Sudan: Death Toll Rises to 160, Al Jazeera Reports
body:
A wave of unmanned‑aircraft strikes has swept across Sudan in recent days, leaving more than 160 people dead and dozens more injured, according to local medics and human‑rights organisations. The most recent assault hit the capital, Khartoum, where three children were killed in a single strike on Monday, underscoring the growing danger to civilians as the conflict between rival military factions intensifies and the use of drones becomes increasingly commonplace.

The surge in aerial attacks follows a pattern that began in early April when the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) first clashed over control of the country’s political transition. While ground battles have dominated headlines, satellite imagery and eyewitness accounts now reveal that both sides are deploying commercially available quad‑copter and fixed‑wing drones to deliver explosives, conduct surveillance and target infrastructure. Human‑rights groups say the lack of clear identification marks on the aircraft makes attribution difficult, but the frequency and scale of the strikes suggest a coordinated escalation rather than isolated incidents.

Medical facilities have borne the brunt of the onslaught. In Khartoum’s Al‑Shaab Hospital, doctors reported a sudden influx of patients with shrapnel wounds and burns after a drone bomb detonated near the emergency department. Similar reports emerged from Omdurman, where a residential block was hit, collapsing several apartments and trapping families under rubble. “We are overwhelmed,” said Dr. Fatima Abdelrahman, the hospital’s chief surgeon. “Our supplies are running low, and we have no way of knowing where the next strike will land.” The health sector, already crippled by shortages of medicine and electricity, now faces the added strain of treating mass‑casualty events in an environment where safe evacuation routes are scarce.

International observers have warned that the unchecked proliferation of drone technology could prolong the conflict and exacerbate civilian suffering. The United Nations Panel of Experts on Sudan has highlighted that the ease of acquiring off‑the‑shelf drone components—often through online marketplaces—allows non‑state actors to field lethal aerial weapons with minimal training. Moreover, the absence of a robust regulatory framework in Sudan means that these devices can be modified to carry improvised explosive devices, turning hobbyist equipment into potent tools of war. Rights groups are calling for an urgent UN‑mandated cease‑fire that specifically bans the use of unmanned aerial systems against populated areas, as well as for the establishment of a verification mechanism to monitor compliance.

Regional dynamics further complicate the situation. Neighboring Egypt and Ethiopia have both expressed concern that the escalation could spill over borders, threatening trade routes and humanitarian corridors that deliver aid to millions of Sudanese displaced by the fighting. Meanwhile, the United States and European Union have imposed limited sanctions on individuals linked to the procurement of drone parts, but critics argue that these measures are insufficient to curb the flow of technology. “Without a coordinated international response, the drone threat will only grow,” said Ahmed El‑Mansour, a senior analyst at the African Policy Institute.

As the death toll climbs, the humanitarian community is urging all parties to prioritize civilian protection and to open channels for dialogue. The World Health Organization has appealed for a protected corridor to deliver medical supplies, while the International Committee of the Red Cross is preparing to negotiate temporary cease‑fires to allow evacuation of the wounded. The coming weeks will test whether diplomatic pressure can rein in the drone campaign or whether the conflict will settle into a grim new normal where unmanned weapons dominate the battlefield, leaving civilians perpetually vulnerable.
